Intesa is counting on completing its offer by the end of December, before MPS has a chance to launch its own bids. COULD UNICREDIT MAKE A MOVE? UniCredit's 9% Generali stake has given it sway in the Intesa-MPS battle. Now that its two-year pursuit of Commerzbank (CBKG.DE) has left it with de facto control of the German lender, UniCredit could refocus on Italy, where it has so far failed to make a mark in the consolidation wave, bankers said. UniCredit CEO Andrea Orcel has said he may forego domestic acquisitions rather than overpay. Bankers don't expect Orcel to disrupt Intesa's plans directly, and instead view Banco BPM and Banca Generali as potential targets for UniCredit. WHAT'S THE GOVERNMENT'S STANCE? The government has maintained [USN:L8N44W0N8 TEXT:"a neutral position"] in the latest banking tussle and is not expected to participate in the October vote with its remaining 4.9% stake in MPS. ($1 = 0.8603 euros)

item.title: JD.com's Ceconomy concessions face criticism from rivals, sources say
item.description: JD.com's concessions to ease EU subsidy concerns about the Chinese e-commerce giant's $2.5 billion purchase of German electronics retailer Ceconomy have prompted criticism from competitors, people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
item.dc:creator: Yun Chee Foo
item.content:encoded: JD.com's (9618.HK) concessions to ease EU subsidy concerns about the Chinese e-commerce giant's $2.5 billion purchase of German electronics retailer Ceconomy (CECG.DE) have prompted criticism from competitors, people familiar with the matter told Reuters. They said the European Commission, which acts as the European Union's competition enforcer, informed JD.com earlier this week of the responses to [USN:L1N44H0JY TEXT:"concessions it offered"] last month. The Commission, which will decide on the deal by October 23, and JD.com declined to comment on the negative feedback, which will put pressure on JD.com to improve its concessions. Under its proposals, Ceconomy would access JD.com's European logistics capability and technological capability at market rates, one of the people said. Smaller rivals would also get access at fair and non-discriminatory rates. The EU antitrust watchdog is examining JD.com's proposed acquisition of Ceconomy under the Foreign Subsidies Regulation that targets unfair foreign state aid. Its preliminary review in May indicated that JD.com may have received foreign subsidies such as preferential financing, tax incentives and grants provided by entities possibly attributable to Beijing. The Commission underscored its misgivings by setting out specific concerns in July, which JD.com will have to address in order to gain approval for the deal.

item.title: Monedas cierran mixtas tras datos EEUU que refuerzan apuestas a alza de tasas Fed
item.description: Las principales monedas de América Latina tuvieron un desempeño dispar al cierre del jueves, en medio de un avance global del dólar tras datos que reforzaron las expectativas de un aumento en las tasas por parte de la Reserva Federal de Estados Unidos (Fed), en su reunión de política monetaria de la próxima semana.
item.dc:creator: Froilan Romero
item.content:encoded: Las principales monedas de América Latina tuvieron un desempeño dispar al cierre del jueves, en medio de un avance global del dólar tras datos que reforzaron las expectativas de un aumento en las tasas por parte de la Reserva Federal de Estados Unidos (Fed), en su reunión de política monetaria de la próxima semana. * Los operadores reforzaron sus apuestas a que la Fed subirá las tasas de interés a corto plazo en su reunión de la próxima semana después de que el primer informe clave de inflación de esta semana revelara que los precios al productor en Estados Unidos subieron un 5,4% en los 12 meses hasta agosto. * Las probabilidades de que el banco central estadounidense eleve los tipos de interés un cuarto de punto en su reunión del 15 al 16 de septiembre subieron al 70%, según el precio de los contratos de futuros sobre fondos federales negociados en CME Group, desde un 65% antes del dato. * El Departamento de Trabajo reportó que el número de estadounidenses que solicitaron prestaciones por desempleo descendió la semana pasada, lo que sugiere que los despidos se mantuvieron en niveles bajos y siguieron estabilizando el mercado laboral. * La atención de los mercados se centra ahora en los datos de agosto del índice de precios al consumidor (IPC) que se darán a conocer el viernes en Estados Unidos y que es considerado clave para la decisión de la Fed en materia de tasas de interés. * El índice dólar , que compara a la divisa frente a una canasta de seis monedas de primer orden, escaló alrededor de un 0,2%. * El peso chileno , anotó la mayor caída al ceder un 1,28% y cerrar en 939,80/940,10 por dólar, presionado, además, por una fuerte caída en los precios del cobre, el mayor envío del país. En tanto, el principal índice de la bolsa de comercio de Santiago, el IPSA (.SPIPSA) , perdió un 1,16%, a 11.238,58 puntos. * Los precios del cobre retrocedieron casi un 4% en Londres tras alcanzar un máximo histórico, mientras los operadores sopesan si el repunte de septiembre se había extendido en exceso tras cinco sesiones de avances impulsados por la preocupación ante la reducción de las existencias fuera de Estados Unidos. * El peso mexicano cotizaba al cierre en 16,9996 unidades por dólar, con una pérdida de un 0,64% frente a los 16,8907 pesos del precio de referencia de LSEG del miércoles, debido a un fortalecimiento global del dólar. * El principal índice accionario S&P/BMV IPC (.MXX) , que integran las 35 empresas más líquidas del mercado mexicano, bajaba un 1,09%, a 64.1105,20 unidades, arrastrado principalmente por firmas del sector minero ante una caída de los precios de los metales. * El real brasileño se apreció un 0,20%, a 5,1013 unidades por dólar, mientras que el índice Bovespa (.BVSP) de la bolsa B3 de Sao Paulo avanzó un 1,42%, a 188.258,29 puntos. * [USN:L6N4520ZO TEXT:"La actividad del sector"] de servicios de Brasil se mantuvo estable en julio respecto del mes anterior, según datos publicados el jueves por la agencia de estadística IBGE, lo que no cumplió con las expectativas y refuerza los indicios de una desaceleración en la mayor economía de América Latina. * En Argentina, el peso cerró en el mercado interbancario con una apreciación de 0,07% a 1.513 unidades por dólar. La moneda local tocó su nivel mínimo intradiario en la sesión previa al marcar las 1.517,5 unidades para la venta. * En tanto, el índice bursátil Merval (.MERV) de la Bolsa de Buenos Aires avanzó un 1,53%, con lo que acumuló un avance de 4,06% en tres sesiones consecutivas de ganancias. Entre las principales alzas se destacó el sector energético. * El Índice de Precios al Consumidor (IPC) de Argentina registró una variación de 1,7% en el octavo mes del año, luego del 2,1% de julio, informó el jueves el Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censos (INDEC), cifra que estuvo en línea con las estimaciones del mercado. * El peso colombiano cambió la tendencia de la apertura de la jornada y cerró con una caída de 0,41%, a 3.090 unidades por dólar, mientras que en la bolsa el índice accionario MSCI COLCAP (.COLCAP) subió 1,65%, a 2.626,71 puntos. * Colombia aumentó en 25 billones de pesos (8.066 millones de dólares) la emisión de títulos de deuda interna para financiar el presupuesto de 2026. El incremento equivale a un 29,3%, desde los 85,25 billones de pesos (27.505 millones de dólares) aprobados inicialmente, de acuerdo con el decreto firmado por el ministro de Hacienda, Miguel Gómez. * La moneda peruana, el sol , cerró la jornada con una merma de 0,51%, a 3,3720/3,3740 unidades por dólar. Por su parte, la Bolsa de Lima (.MXNUAMPESCPGPE) caía un 1,61%, a 1.559,28 puntos.

item.title: White House says it will send $500 Obamacare refunds to nearly a million Americans
item.description: The White House said on Thursday it will send $500 to nearly one million Americans in 30 states who are enrolled in Obamacare health insurance plans, payments it described as refunds for overcharges.
item.dc:creator: Ahmed Aboulenein, Yasmeen Abutaleb
item.content:encoded: The White House said on Thursday it will send $500 to nearly one million Americans in 30 states who are enrolled in Obamacare health insurance plans, payments it described as refunds for overcharges. It said "user fees" passed on to consumers in the form of higher premiums by the administration of President Joe Biden were in excess of what was needed to run the federal exchange, or Healthcare.gov. Obamacare plans, created by Democratic President Barack Obama's signature Affordable Care Act, offer subsidies based on income. Republican President Donald Trump sought unsuccessfully in his first term to overturn the law and has proposed changes that would make the plans less comprehensive. Millions of [USN:L1N41O16Y TEXT:"people dropped coverage"] this year as rising medical costs and the expiration of extra COVID-era subsidies made monthly premiums unaffordable. People on the higher end of the income scale who lost those subsidies were among the hardest hit. The White House said checks to eligible Americans will begin going out in October. Health insurers who offer plans under the ACA on Healthcare.gov pay the government a user fee to sell plans on the federal exchange, set annually by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services as a percentage of premiums. According to a White House official, the $500 refund will primarily go to people earning more than 400% of the federal poverty level who do not qualify for subsidies, as well as those earning between 100% and 400% who did not receive subsidies. The administration has already identified eligible recipients, it said. The official confirmed that these payments are unrelated to the [USN:L6N452119 TEXT:"$5,000 payment"] Trump announced on Wednesday night should his Republican party retain control of Congress in November's midterm elections. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The states involved in the payments, most of which are Republican-led, are Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Delaware, Florida, Hawaii, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, West Virginia, Wisconsin and Wyoming. USER FEES The user fees help pay for the Healthcare.gov website, its call center and grants to "navigator" groups that assist people in enrolling in the plans, said Cynthia Cox, director of the ACA program at KFF, a health policy research group. The fee is set roughly a year in advance. The 1.5% rate for 2025 and the 2.5% rate for the current 2026 plan year were both finalized by the Biden administration, which projected higher fees to offset an expected enrollment drop when the COVID subsidies expired. The Trump administration's first payment rule, issued in May, cut the fee to 1.9% for 2027. Insurers build the fee into premiums, so consumers do not see it as a separate charge. A surplus does not mean consumers were overcharged, Cox said, attributing it largely to the current administration's decision to cut spending on programs like the navigators while continuing to collect the fee. The rationale for limiting refunds to unsubsidized enrollees is that subsidized enrollees have their payments capped as a share of income, Cox explained, so higher premiums are largely absorbed by the government. Cox said she knew of no precedent for refunding user fees to consumers, though the government issues other rebates regularly.

item.title: Fed, eyeing inflation data, may lean toward a hike, traders bet
item.description: The Federal Reserve is a bit more likely to raise short-term borrowing costs at its meeting next week, traders bet on Thursday, after the first of this week's key inflation reports.
item.dc:creator: Ann Saphir
item.content:encoded: The Federal Reserve is a bit more likely to raise short-term borrowing costs at its meeting next week, traders bet on Thursday, after the first of this week's key inflation reports. Data showed U.S. [USN:L1N4500SJ TEXT:"producer prices"] rose 5.4% in the 12 months through August, and the country's weekly [USN:L1N4500R4 TEXT:"unemployment insurance claims"] indicated the job market remains stable. Though the overall increase in wholesale prices was in line with what economists had projected, details in the Producer Price Index suggested some of the recent slowing of inflation is being undone as renewed hostilities in the Middle East crimp global oil distribution and the surge in AI investment pushes up demand for electronics. Prices that producers paid for transportation and warehousing jumped in August, the data showed, as did prices for hospital services and airfares. CONSUMER PRICE INDEX IN FOCUS A report on consumer price inflation due on Friday will fill out the inflation picture for Fed officials as they debate whether their policy rate is putting enough downward pressure on inflation to get it to their 2% goal. Inflation has run above the Fed's target for 5-1/2 years. The Fed has kept its policy rate in the 3.50%-3.75% range since December. "With the PPI data overall still looking relatively hot, the Fed seems likely to hike this year even if it doesn’t pull the trigger this month," Capital Economics analysts wrote. As for whether the central bank moves next week, they said, "that still depends on the more important core CPI figure tomorrow." The Fed targets 2% inflation by 12-month change in the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, a data point that can be estimated once CPI and PPI data are in hand. Analysts were divided on Thursday over whether PPI data would push PCE inflation into a range high enough to force the Fed to move next week. Before Thursday's data, traders had seen about a 65% chance of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed's September 15-16 meeting. That probability is now seen as closer to 70%, based on the price of Fed funds futures contracts traded at CME Group. By year-end, the Fed will almost certainly have delivered one, if not two, interest-rate hikes, market prices imply. The European Central Bank raised its key interest rates earlier on Thursday to stem inflation arising from the Iran war, which has pushed Brent oil futures prices above $100 a barrel.

item.title: US CPI, where the significant and the silly collide
item.description: Is it too cliched to say that the next U.S. inflation report will be the most important since the last one? Maybe, but the consumer price index (CPI) data for August is shaping up to have a hugely significant bearing on Federal Reserve policy, potentially sealing the case for an interest rate rise next week and the resumption of a monetary tightening cycle.
item.dc:creator: Jamie McGeever
item.content:encoded: Is it too cliched to say that the next U.S. inflation report will be the most important since the [USN:L1N4480XR TEXT:"last one"]? Maybe, but the consumer price index (CPI) data for August is shaping up to have a hugely significant bearing on [USN:L1N4480XR TEXT:"Federal Reserve policy"], potentially sealing the case for an interest rate rise next week and the resumption of a monetary tightening cycle. The prospect of one data point having such an outsized impact on Fed policy is puzzling, given that Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said in his Jackson Hole speech that policymakers shouldn't rely on "isolated data points" and that "trends matter most." Plus, CPI isn't even the Fed's favored measure of inflation — that's the annual rate of change in the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) index. That the decision to raise the most important central bank policy rate in the world could boil down to the second, or even third, decimal place in a month-on-month inflation figure just adds to the circus. But here we are. A confluence of events — huge uncertainty around Fed communications, Warsh's rocky start to his tenure, a bond market rout, and some curveball signaling from influential Governor Christopher Waller — has dramatically raised the stakes around the Bureau of Labor Statistics' August CPI report, due at 8:30 a.m. ET (1330 GMT) on Friday. ALL WE ARE SAYING The consensus estimates in a [USN:S0N4490CS TEXT:"Reuters poll"] of economists for the four key numbers are: monthly headline and core inflation of 0.4% and 0.2%, respectively; annual headline and core inflation of 3.4% and 2.4%, respectively. Speaking at a Reuters event last week, Waller said that if inflation "comes in hot", he would consider voting for a rate hike at the Fed's September 15 to 16 policy meeting. But what would constitute "hot"? A monthly core print of 0.2% in line with consensus wouldn't cut it, and would likely give sufficient cover for the Federal Open Market Committee to sit tight and, to quote Waller again, "[USN:S0N4490CF TEXT:"give disinflation a chance."]" On the other hand, 0.4% core would clearly be "hot" and would tip the balance for Waller and probably many of his colleagues on the FOMC. But would 0.3%? And what difference, if any, would it make if the figure was 0.251% or 0.349%? After all, both would be rounded to 0.3%. Or, would a month-on-month rise of 0.251% seal the deal for a hike, but 0.249% signal no change? It seems faintly silly to be drilling down to the third decimal place. But many economists' month-on-month CPI estimates are to the second decimal point, and you can be sure the figures will be sliced and diced in every way possible after their release. COMMUNICATION BREAKDOWN Part of the problem is the communications void that has mushroomed since Warsh took the hot seat at the end of May. This is ironic, given that he vowed to simplify and improve communication. But Warsh has been reluctant to reveal his thinking on the Fed's "reaction function", how the central bank will adjust policy depending on changes in inflation and employment. He has been even more vehement in his disdain for "forward guidance" — clearer signals or commitments on the path for interest rates — yet that is exactly what a growing clutch of Fed officials have ended up giving. Tim Duy, chief U.S. economist at SGH Macro Advisors, says Waller's remarks last week made the September meeting "heavily data-point dependent". This surely isn't the direction Warsh wants to take the Fed. But critics say he has allowed the fog around communication and the central bank's reaction function to thicken, leaving markets increasingly confused. Waller's input last week wasn't particularly helpful either, economists say. Of course, one could argue that the decision to raise rates will ultimately be rooted in the multi-month trends on both sides of the Fed’s mandate, regardless of whether this one data point tips the scale. But if CPI comes in slightly “cool” and forestalls a hike, that argument will be harder to support given that the U.S. is at full employment and inflation has been above target for five and a half years. Rates traders are now leaning 65-35 towards a rate hike next week. Watch those decimal places. (The opinions expressed here are those of the author, a columnist for Reuters) Enjoying this column?
